problems.stem: Your prototype trains warehouse staff with low LMS experience, but you recruit 5 instructional designers because they are available. What is the main threat to your usability evidence?
options: The sample is too small for any conclusion.
Expert designers will not encounter the friction the real low-experience users would, so usability problems stay hidden.
Designers cannot give honest feedback about their own field.
You should always recruit exactly 8 participants.
problems.explanation: A convenience sample of experts is unrepresentative of the target population, so it hides the very problems the test should surface.

problems.stem: Which screening criterion best targets the design risk in a tutoring prototype whose hardest moment is first-time onboarding?
options: Recruit whoever responds first to the email.
Recruit only people who already use the tutoring tool daily.
Screen on prior experience with similar tools and include a band of first-time users who face the onboarding step.
problems.explanation: Screen on the trait that drives the design risk; first-time users are the ones who will reveal onboarding friction.

problems.stem: An AI tool generates synthetic participant personas and offers to 'run' the usability session against them. What is the defensible boundary?
options: Replace real recruitment with the AI personas to save time.
Use the personas only to draft your screener and profile categories, then test with real humans from the target population.
Trust the AI session results because the personas are detailed.
Avoid AI personas entirely because sampling must be manual.
problems.explanation: Synthetic personas can scaffold a screener, but usability evidence requires observed behavior from real members of the population.

problems.stem: A team recruits 6 frequent users of the platform, finds almost no problems, and concludes the design works for all learners. Why does this overclaim?
options: Six participants is statistically significant, so the claim is fine.
The sample covers only one slice of learner variability; results cannot generalize to first-time or occasional users who were never observed.
They should have run an A/B test instead.
Frequent users always find more problems, not fewer.
problems.explanation: A sample that omits parts of the population's variability cannot support a claim about the whole population.
